hints: Look at the dashed left ventricle line just before it shoots steeply upwards at about 0.2 s. Compare it to the dotted left atrium line in the narrow period labelled A.

Remember blood only flows into the ventricle when atrial pressure is higher than ventricular pressure with the AV valve open, so the ventricle is fullest just before ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure to start contraction.
walkthrough:
**Spot what fills the ventricle**

Think simply first. The left ventricle fills from the left atrium when the atrium has higher pressure than the ventricle. That keeps the AV (bicuspid) valve open.

Filling rule:
$$P_{atrium} > P_{ventricle} \text{ means AV valve open and filling}$$

**Read the graph around A**

In period A, both atrial (dotted) and ventricular (dashed) pressures are very low. You can see a small bump in atrial pressure just before 0.2 s. This is atrial systole squeezing the last bit of blood into the ventricle.

**Find the moment of maximum fullness**

Right at the end of A, the dashed ventricular line shoots almost vertically upwards. That sharp rise means ventricular systole is starting and pressure will soon close the AV valve. So just before that rise, filling has finished and the ventricle is full.

options.A: Correct. The end of A is the end of atrial systole and ventricular diastole, just before ventricular contraction, so the ventricle contains its maximum volume.
options.B: False. In B ventricular pressure is rising sharply above atrial and aortic pressure, so the ventricle is contracting and ejecting blood, not filling.
options.C: False. In C ventricular pressure is high then falling rapidly, which is late ejection, so the ventricle is emptying and is nearly empty by the end.
options.D: False. D is early to mid diastole with passive filling from the atrium, but the final top-up from atrial systole has not yet happened, so the ventricle is not yet completely full.
